title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) Guide | Clumio by Commvault
summary: Learn what recovery time objective means, how RTO vs RPO differ, and how to calculate and help improve your RTO targets for disaster recovery planning.
body_markdown:
## Improve RTO


Setting an RTO is only useful if you can actually hit it. Here are the strategies that consistently reduce recovery time.


**Adopt cloud-based disaster recovery.** Cloud DR helps eliminate the need to maintain idle standby hardware. On-demand infrastructure lets you spin up recovery environments in minutes, not hours. According to the Uptime Institute’s[Annual Outage Analysis 2025](https://uptimeinstitute.com/resources/research-and-reports/annual-outage-analysis-2025) , organizations that have adopted cloud-based DR and automated failover report measurably shorter outage durations compared to those relying on traditional approaches. Review these[cloud disaster recovery best practices](https://www.commvault.com/blogs/three-cloud-disaster-recovery-best-practices) for a deeper look at implementation.


**Implement continuous replication.** Point-in-time snapshots taken hours apart create data gaps that inflate both RPO and RTO. Continuous replication helps to keep standby environments current, so recovery starts from a near-real-time state.


**Automate failover and validation.** Manual recovery steps introduce human error and delay. Automated runbooks execute failover sequences, verify data integrity, and confirm service availability – all without waiting for an on-call engineer to step through a wiki page at 3 a.m.


**Test regularly and measure.** A recovery plan that has never been tested is a hypothesis, not a plan. Run DR drills quarterly. Measure actual recovery time against your RTO. Document gaps and fix them before they matter.
